title: Efficient learning of quantum interactions from thermal metastable states
authors: Bingrun Wang, Qi Ye, Chi-Fang Chen
abstract: Learning quantum interactions from finite-temperature many-body systems is a central task in emerging quantum platforms. Recently, the problem of learning from lattice quantum Gibbs states has found rigorous, efficient protocols. Nevertheless, exact Gibbs states, as the input premise, are in fact computationally intractable to prepare and may not faithfully represent generic finite-temperature quantum systems. In contrast, a system coupled to a heat bath can be stuck at an approximate stationary state (metastable state) long before it truly equilibrates. Here, we formulate a physically and algorithmically consistent alternative: learning from such metastable states of detailed-balanced master equations (Lindbladians) arising from system-bath interactions. We distill the algorithmic mechanism and structural condition underlying Gibbs-state learning and extend it in full to metastable states, attaining nearly optimal sample and computational complexity (in the system size and the precision). More broadly, we sharpen notions of metastability and develop a unified framework for finite-temperature learning.
summary: This paper develops a general framework for learning quantum interactions from metastable states rather than requiring the computationally intractable exact Gibbs states. By exploiting the concept of Approximate Detailed Balance, the authors extend existing efficient learning protocols to these realistic, non-equilibrium inputs. This provides a powerful, unified method for characterizing complex quantum dynamics from limited measurements.
main_problem: The central task is learning the unknown quantum interactions (Hamiltonian) governing a many-body system from measurements taken on finite-temperature, non-equilibrium metastable states.
main_result: The authors establish a unified framework showing that the Hamiltonian can be learned from metastable states using the same efficient protocols developed for true Gibbs states, achieving near-optimal complexity.
method: The approach extends established Gibbs-state learning protocols to metastable states by leveraging the concept of Approximate Detailed Balance (ADB). It uses local measurements on these metastable states to iteratively estimate Hamiltonian coefficients.
model_or_system: The system is an $n$-qubit lattice governed by a Hamiltonian $H$ and evolves under a Lindbladian master equation $L[\sigma]$. The input data consists of $\epsilon$-metastable states $\sigma$, which are approximate stationary points ($\|L[\sigma]\|_1 \le \epsilon$) but not necessarily the true Gibbs state.
key_observables: Hamiltonian coefficients ($h_\gamma$), expectation values $	ext{Tr}(M_\sigma)$, and the degree of non-equilibrium ($\|L[\sigma]\|_1$).
important_parameters: Inverse temperature ($ eta$), metastability error ($\epsilon$), and desired estimation precision ($\eta$).
main_assumptions: The system dynamics are modeled by a weak-coupling, time-Markovian Lindbladian, and the input states are sufficiently metastable to exhibit Approximate Detailed Balance (ADB).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates that a metastable state can be far from equilibrium but still approximately stationary, demonstrating that metastability implies Approximate Detailed Balance (ADB), which underpins the iterative learning algorithm.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by first defining the problem in terms of metastable states, then extending the known Gibbs-state learning mechanisms to this new input class, and finally deriving the complexity bounds for the estimation process.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides a robust theoretical tool for characterizing and learning the dynamics of complex, non-equilibrium quantum systems, which are common in open quantum systems and thermalization studies.
